Peg Solitaire

Game StrategyInvariants

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: jump a peg over a neighbour into an empty hole; the jumped peg comes off. Clear the board down to one peg in the middle (or reverse the start).
How to play: click a peg, then the hole it should land in. Use Undo to take back a jump.
Look for the math

Peg solitaire on the English board looks like a long search, but whole runs of jumps can be packed into short recipes. Winning Ways sells them as packages and purges.

Jumps and the English board

The board is a 7×7 square with the four corner 2×2 blocks cut away — thirty-three holes. A move is an orthogonal jump of length two over a peg into an empty hole; the jumped peg is removed. Each jump lowers the peg count by one, so the usual central start (thirty-two pegs, empty centre) needs thirty-one jumps to finish with a single peg. The logic test rebuilds every applet layout from the bytecode and checks that Cross, the smallest centre-goal puzzle, really is solvable.

Packages and purges

Berlekamp, Conway and Guy's 3-purge clears three pegs in a line when a catalyst peg and hole sit beside the head: one jump borrows the catalyst, a second clears the line, and a third restores the catalyst. Larger purges (6-purge, L-purge) are built from the same idea. The page's packaged solution of the central puzzle is two 3-purges, three 6-purges, an L-purge, and a final jump — each with its catalyst in place.

Centre or reverse

Most of the applet's layouts ask for a single peg at the centre. Skewed and Double goal instead use the applet's reverse test: every hole that began with a peg must be empty. (The bytecode does not also demand that former holes become pegs.) Design your own lets you place pegs and pick the Centre goal with the checkbox, as in the applet.

Try Cross first — six pegs, and the same jump rule as the full board.
